plan: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy regardless of the number of bidders or their strategies. This is because your payment (if you win) depends only on the second-highest bid, not your own bid, so there's no incentive to shade your bid. Bidding above your value risks winning and overpaying (paying more than your value if you're not truly the highest valuer relative to price), while bidding below risks losing profitable opportunities. Therefore, I should bid exactly my value of $32.

In a second-price auction, bidding your true value is the dominant strategy since you pay the second-highest bid, not your own bid. Bidding higher than my value risks paying more than the item is worth to me; bidding lower risks losing auctions I could profitably win. With a value of $6, the optimal strategy is straightforward: bid exactly $6 regardless of what I expect others to bid.

This is a second-price sealed-bid auction with 3 bidders and uniform values on [0,49]. The optimal strategy (Nash equilibrium) in this setting is to bid a fraction of my true value, specifically bid = value * (n-1)/n = value * 2/3, since truthful bidding isn't optimal in second-price auctions with common priors when bidders shade bids strategically... actually in second-price auctions, truthful bidding IS the dominant strategy regardless of others' behavior. I should bid my true value of $17.
